title: Christian Pulisic’s Role in New Look USMNT Hinges on One Thing
subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Sukhman Singh7:00 AM ESTWhat does the future hold for Pulisic? /  Maja Hitij/FIFA/Getty ImagesChristian Pulisic is back with the U.S. men’s national team for the Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals, entering the November international window in a rich vein of form: four goals in six Serie A starts.

His last national team appearance ended early in the World Cup round of 16, when a microfracture of the tibia and fibula in his right leg against Belgium cost him Milan's preseason and the start of the domestic campaign. By the time USMNT’s September-October roster was announced, Pulisic had just one half of first team minutes to his name, as a substitute against Lazio.

He was overlooked in the 28-man roster for the four fall friendlies. The omission was partly down to fitness and a lack of minutes, but Mauricio Pochettino was also signalling his ambition for the next World Cup cycle. The Argentine used this window to widen the pool, with burgeoning teenage talents, such as Cavan Sullivan, Julian Hall and Justin Ellis, earning meaningful minutes in the national shirt in the absence of big names.
With Pochettino reportedly high on the wanted list of Manchester United should they replace Michael Carrick imminently, as expected, Pulisic could actually have a new national manager.
But whoever leads the USMNT in this next cycle, the question remains: Where does Pulisic fit into this new edition of the USMNT? Does he, in fact, fit at all?

Weston McKennie (left), Pulisic and Antonee Robinson (right) were three core members of the “golden generation.” / Al Sermeno/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesFor the better part of the last decade, Pulisic has been the poster boy of an American generation expected to take U.S. Soccer to unprecedented heights. With 90 caps, 33 goals and a decade at three of Europe’s biggest clubs, he remains the pool’s most experienced attacker and its biggest global star. For the 2030 World Cup cycle, though, the team is no longer being built around him.

This long-anticipated “golden generation,” which also includes the likes of Weston McKennie, Tyler Adams and Antonee Robinson, was forged in European academies, rather than domestic ones. The share of non-MLS players on the World Cup roster has climbed from 57% in 2014 to 69% in 2026, and roughly 10 members of the 2022 roster came through European academies as teenagers. Pulisic was the first to catch the eye, and his performances have been the most visible of them all.

Pochettino’s September-October camp leaned heavily into MLS, accounting for 12 of the initial 28 selections and rising to 13, or 46%, after Damion Downs replaced the injured Ricardo Pepi. But the long-term structural trajectory remains nuanced. The November roster pulled the MLS contingent back to a familiar 32%, nearly identical to the World Cup roster. The broader philosophical shift is still undeniable: three of the roster’s five selected forwards are young MLS prospects, proof that Pochettino's youth-centric recalculation of the frontline has endured.

Viz 1: Where the World Cup roster was built. / ussoccerplayers.comHowever the pipeline shifts, the home World Cup was where the European-forged generation was expected to deliver. It began with discipline and promise and ended against Belgium in frustration and another round of 16 exit. Pulisic’s second World Cup was goalless and injury-ridden. He now has one goal in eight World Cup appearances.

For a player widely regarded as the most talented the USMNT has ever produced, that record reads as an unfulfilled promise. He is often placed alongside Landon Donovan and Clint Dempsey in stature. Has he lived up to the comparison?

Viz 2: International goals by competition, career to date / FbrefSet against the two veterans, Pulisic’s case is a mixed one. Their per-cap scoring rates are near identical, and friendlies account for a similar share of each player’s goals, so none of them padded their numbers against minnows.

The gap is in the tournaments. Donovan scored 44% of his international goals in tournament finals, Dempsey 40%, Pulisic 24%. Pulisic’s scoring instead sits in qualifying, which accounts for 36% of his goals, against 23% for Donovan and 32% for Dempsey. The World Cup gap is the widest of all: Donovan and Dempsey scored 0.42 and 0.40 goals per World Cup cap, Pulisic 0.13.

The numbers go against him on the biggest stage. He has carried his side through qualifying, but World Cup goals remain unfinished business. That is where Donovan and Dempsey built their reputations, and where Pulisic has not.

Cavan Sullivan is one of the USMNT’s most promising stars. / Omar Vega/USSF/Getty ImagesWhere Pulisic fits in this next World Cup cycle has become a tactical puzzle.

After the November roster announcement, Pochettino explained the attack he had just picked. “I think the combination between [Folarin] Balogun, [Justin] Ellis and [Julian] Hall is perfect,” he said. Balogun, like Pulisic, had missed the September-October friendlies, and it was in his absence the teenagers made their case: Ellis, Hall and Sullivan scored half of the dozen goals across those four games, all three fully fit whereas Pepi was not.

What Pochettino praised was as much the mentality as the finishing. He called Sullivan “a fighter” and “a warrior,” singled out the group’s willingness to chase and recover the ball and paired the praise with a reminder to keep “both feet on the ground.”

The U.S. won all four friendlies by spreading the attacking load rather than isolating wingers. They played through the middle, with a group of young strikers and a set of creative playmakers behind them, and the goals came from quick, short combinations in half-spaces.

Again and again, the post-World Cup postmortems landed on the same complaint: American soccer was waiting, once more, for one player to lift the program. The autumn windows read as a deliberate attempt to break the habit.
